items.title: A possible condition or an imagined opposite

states.label: May yet happen
states.sm: ʻĀfai ʻe te lē sau, ʻou te alu atu.
states.en: If you do not come, I will go and see you.
states.note: The listener may still come or not come.

states.label: Did not happen
states.sm: ʻAna ʻe lē sau, semanū ʻou te alu atu.
states.en: Had you not come, I was probably going to go and see you.
states.note: The listener did come. The speaker imagines the not-coming instead.

items.caption: Three things change together: the if-word, the missing *te* in the condition, and *semanū* in the main clause. The condition after *ʻana* usually has no tense particle.

items.title: Put the imagined condition second

states.label: Condition first
states.sm: ʻAna ʻe lē sau, ʻou te ita.
states.en: Had you not come, I would have been angry.

states.label: Condition second
states.sm: ʻOu te ita pē ʻana ʻe lē sau.
states.en: I would have been angry if you had not come.

items.caption: When the condition follows the main clause, *pē* stands in front of *ʻana*. The imagined situation stays the same.

items.title: Does the second situation stop the first?

items.sm: ʻOu te sāvali i le aoga seʻiloga e timu.
items.en: I walk to school, unless it rains.
items.why: Rain is the exception that stops the walk from holding true.

items.sm: E ui ina faigatā le feau, ʻae ʻou te fiafia.
items.en: Although the task is difficult, I am happy.
items.why: The happiness holds despite what the difficult task might lead someone to expect.

items.sm: Tīgā ona ʻou ole atu i loʻu tina, ʻae na lē mafai ona ʻou alu.
items.en: However much I begged my mother, I could not go.
items.why: The main clause holds despite the begging. *Tīgā* presents the contrast as a negative idea.

items.sm: E lē alu le malaga seʻiloga ʻua sau le tama.
items.en: The trip will not go unless the boy has come.
items.why: The boy’s coming is the exception to the trip not going.

items.intro: Choose between a condition that makes an exception and a contrast that still holds.

items.title: The question clause decides the reading

states.label: One condition
states.sm: E tusa pē timu, ʻae ʻoleʻā alu le malaga.
states.en: Even if it rains, the trip will go.
states.note: One condition is named, and the trip holds despite it.

states.label: Both answers
states.sm: ʻOleʻā alu le malaga e tusa lava pē timu pē leai.
states.en: The trip will go whether it rains or not.
states.note: Both raining and not raining are named; either answer leaves the trip unchanged.

states.label: An open answer
states.sm: E tatalo le tama, tusa lava po ʻo fea le nuʻu ʻo i ai.
states.en: The boy prays, whatever village he is in.
states.note: The question leaves the village open, and the praying holds wherever it is.

items.caption: The English follows the question after *tusa*: even if, whether or not, or whatever. *Lava* belongs in the last two patterns; it is optional in the even-if pattern.
